articles.title: Why the US Air Force Is Looking at a Hybrid-Electric Aircraft for Special Forces
articles.text:
Electra Defense today announced it has received a $4.7 million innovative capabilities opening (ICO) contract award from the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) to advance hybrid-electric aircraft power and propulsion technologies through a comprehensive program of ground testing and flight testing.
The ICO will support testing and evaluation of Electra’s EL9 aircraft and its hybrid-electric propulsion systems, generating critical performance data to help the U.S. Air Force assess the potential of next-generation ultra-short takeoff and landing (Ultra-STOL) aircraft for military operations. The effort will also examine how hybrid-electric aviation can expand operational access, strengthen distributed logistics, and support the Air Force’s Agile Combat Employment (ACE) doctrine.
The $4.7 million award marks the latest development in Electra’s longstanding partnership with AFRL to advance hybrid-electric aviation technologies for military applications. In 2023, Electra received a Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) award valued at up to $85 million to support development of its full-scale preproduction aircraft. That collaboration has since included flight demonstrations and government-directed testing, most recently during AFRL’s Future Flag 25-3 exercise in 2025, where Electra demonstrated the potential of Ultra-STOL aircraft and hybrid-electric propulsion to support runway-independent distributed military operations and mobile power generation.
“This award represents an important step in demonstrating how hybrid-electric aircraft technology can address some of the Air Force’s most pressing operational challenges,” said Donn Yates, Vice President and General Manager of Electra Defense. “Power and propulsion are fundamental to unlocking new capabilities for military aviation. Through this effort, we’re moving to generate real-world aircraft performance data that will help the Air Force evaluate how these technologies can support more agile, distributed, and resilient operations.”
Under the contract, Electra will conduct a series of technical evaluations focused on aircraft performance, hybrid-electric propulsion system functionality, and operational effectiveness. The effort includes verification of key hybrid-electric power and propulsion technologies, extensive ground testing of the EL9 preproduction aircraft, and acoustic flight testing to characterize the ability to conduct battery-only low-signature ingress and egress for special operations missions. These activities will provide the Air Force with insights into aircraft performance and mission effectiveness while advancing technology maturity.
The program will also evaluate the potential operational advantages of hybrid-electric ultra-STOL aircraft through modeling and simulation, including their ability to operate from a wider range of locations, support the rapid dispersal of personnel and time-sensitive cargo, and reduce dependence on traditional aviation infrastructure and ground support equipment. The findings will help inform future Air Force technology development and acquisition decisions.
“Future military operations will demand aircraft that can operate with greater flexibility, access more locations, and reduce the logistical burden on deployed forces,” Yates added. “The combination of hybrid-electric power, distributed propulsion, and Ultra Short takeoff and landing capability offers a fundamentally discriminating approach to tactical mobility. This contract will help us quantify those advantages and demonstrate their potential value to the Air Force.”

articles.title: Moscow Urges Europe to Participate in Ukraine Peace Negotiations
articles.text:
The Kremlin said on Friday that Europe must show it is ready to contribute to the Ukraine peace process before a decision is made on letting Europeans join the negotiations.
The comment by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov suggests Russia has not yet committed to including Europeans in the next round of talks, despite US negotiators saying on Thursday that President Vladimir Putin had agreed to their participation.
The talks have so far involved Russian, Ukrainian and US officials, who met in Abu Dhabi this week for the first time in nine months. Two US envoys then flew to Moscow to meet Putin and later met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Dublin.
Asked if peace talks would soon resume with the added participation of Europeans, Peskov said: “Once we understand their genuine intention and readiness to contribute to the peace process, then it will be possible to make a decision on holding dialogue on a Ukrainian settlement in an expanded format.”
European involvement would mark a new phase in efforts to end the nearly five-year-old conflict, which has defied attempts by US President Donald Trump to secure a peace agreement.
Russia’s relations with European powers are dire. European states have armed Ukraine and imposed sanctions on Moscow, and most have shunned direct contact with Putin since he sent troops to Ukraine in February 2022.Putin said on Thursday the US must work with its European allies to understand whether they wanted peace or war in Ukraine.
Peskov said Moscow would be open to the idea of some form of contacts with Europe before any European participation in peace negotiations, but that no concrete discussions on this had taken place.
Asked how the Kremlin would view French President Emmanuel Macron as a potential interlocutor at peace talks, Peskov said: “Every hour, reports are appearing that name completely different candidates. So for the time being we are not in a position to say anything specific.”
Who Would represent EU?Peskov declined to comment on the possibility of European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas representing the EU at negotiations. Kallas has frequently questioned Russia’s good faith in the peace process and taken a lead in imposing successive waves of sanctions on Moscow.
She said on Friday it was not up to Russia to say who should represent the EU in peace talks.
“They don’t want anybody strong on the other side because they want to push through their maximum demands,” she said.
Russia says it wants a full peace settlement, not a ceasefire. Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this week that Moscow wanted to negotiate a broad European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.Russian and Ukrainian officials said some progress was made at the Abu Dhabi talks, but there was no sign of a major breakthrough on key issues such as territory.
Putin has shown no signs of being ready to moderate his territorial demands, which include a buffer zone in parts of Ukraine which Russia has not formally claimed as its own.
Ukraine has refused Russia’s demands to give up territory in the eastern Ukrainian region of Donbas that it has not lost in fighting.

articles.title: Boeing Brings Artificial Intelligence and Drones Into C-17 Inspections
articles.text:
Boeing Global Services is maturing its drone-based aircraft inspection capability on the C-17 Globemaster III to help modernize how inspections are planned, performed and reviewed.
The Advanced Aircraft Inspection (AAI) program, underway at the San Antonio, Texas, site, combines autonomous drone flight with Boeing’s Automated Damage Detection Software (ADDS) to capture exterior images, identify anomalies and support maintainers with a digital record that can be reviewed and acted on more quickly than traditional methods.
Why it matters: The effort will contribute to technician safety by reducing reliance on manual lift equipment and wing walks and increasing inspection consistency while improving fleet availability. Improving the efficiency of inspections will support fleet availability by reducing the time aircraft spend out of service.
- Boeing has validated core workflows and established the procedures needed to support training, qualification, quality and day-to-day maintenance operations.
What they’re saying: “AAI is about turning innovation into operational value,” said Travis Williams, vice president of Mobility and Surveillance Aircraft Services. “We’re delivering measurable improvements and building a repeatable capability that can be scaled as we validate outcomes.”
What’s next: San Antonio teams continue to advance the processes involved.
- The work supports Boeing’s broader focus on safely improving maintenance flow, strengthening digital records, and creating a path for additional military and commercial applications.
- Global Services government and commercial teams are sharing lessons to accelerate future deployments and improve repeatability.
Leveraging AI: An important part of the effort is the algorithm. As Boeing continues improving ADDS, the software’s ability to identify defects and patterns will grow.
- Over time, its detection capability is expected to improve inspection of lightning damage and early evidence of corrosion. This can reduce downtime, improve operational safety and establish authoritative digital records of aircraft condition.
Big picture: Boeing’s goal is to make AAI a standard maintenance effort deployed widely across company programs and sites, improving how inspections are performed while supporting safety, efficiency, quality, and long-term sustainment and readiness goals for military and civilian customers.

articles.title: Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth Begins Official Visit to Czech Republic
articles.text:
General Dhiraj Seth, Chief of the Army Staff (COAS), proceeded on an official visit to the Czech Republic from 16 to 19 November 2026. The visit aims to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation, enhance military-to-military engagement and explore opportunities for collaboration in defence technology and industry.
During the visit, the COAS will hold discussions with senior military leaders of the Czech Armed Forces, including Lieutenant General Petr Čepelka, First Deputy Chief of the General Staff and the Deputy Chief of Defence at General Staff Headquarters (GSHQ) in Prague. The COAS will pay tribute to fallen soldiers during a wreath-laying ceremony at the GSHQ. He will call on senior officials of the Ministry of Defence. These engagements will focus on matters of mutual interest, including military cooperation, training, modernisation and emerging security challenges.
As part of the programme, General Dhiraj Seth will visit the Defence University in Brno and the NATO Joint Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Defence Centre of Excellence to gain insights into specialised training, operational capabilities and future readiness of the Czech Armed Forces.
The COAS will interact with representatives of Inter-governmental Defence Cooperation Agency (AMOS), the Defence and Security Industry Association and leading defence manufacturers to explore opportunities for cooperation in defence technology and industry.
The visit reflects the shared commitment of India and the Czech Republic to strengthening bilateral defence relations through sustained military dialogue, professional exchanges and industrial partnerships.

articles.title: Indian-Built Avro HS-748 Completes 65 Years Since First Flight
articles.text:
India’s first indigenously assembled Avro HS-748 transport plane completed 65 years since its first flight on 1 November 2026. Named after the country’s first Chief of the Air Staff Air Marshal Subroto Mukerjee, the plane took off from the Indian Air Force’s Aircraft Manufacturing Depot in Kanpur on 1 November 1961.
The plane registered BH-572 holds a special place in the history books of Indian aviation. It was assembled under a licence deal with the Avro manufacturer of Britain (now part of Hawker Siddeley) by the Air Force in Kanpur. It made its first flight, piloted by Air Vice Marshal Harjinder Singh who was pivotal in setting up the plane manufacturing facility. The test pilots Chandu Gole and Ripu Daman Sahni were also on board.
What makes this programme unique is that the manufacturing happened in the Air Force itself. The first four HS-748s were assembled in the Aircraft Manufacturing Depot from parts and major components imported from Britain. In June 1964 it was handed over to Aeronautics India Limited and became a part of Hindustan Aeronautics Limited.
HAL continued manufacturing the HS-748 with the aircraft built in Kanpur being used in the Indian Air Force and other civilian and government bodies. It was supplied to Indian Airlines, National Remote Sensing Agency and the Airports Authority of India.
The HS-748 was chosen to replace the ageing Dakota fleet and provided a good payload, flexible aircraft. It had two Rolls-Royce Dart turboprops making it a common site in both the military and civilian sectors.
The Avro was used by the Indian Air Force for many different roles throughout several decades. It was used for transport, communications, training and more. As told by one IAF veteran it was used by many units including Nos. 11, 33 and 59 Squadrons, communication squadrons and flights, Navigation Training School, Fixed Wing Flying Training, No. 181 Squadron, No. 106 Squadron, Flight Inspection Unit, Aircrew Examination Board and continues to be used by No. 41 Squadron.
It is said that the aircraft has clocked up around 10 lakh flying hours throughout its 6.5 decade career. Whilst there is no central source for the exact number of flying hours the aircraft has completed it shows just how much it contributed to the transport sector.
Interestingly the original Subroto plane has stayed with HAL, repainted in IAF colours and with registration BH-572. It is now used as a corporate plane.
A book has been planned to celebrate the 65th year called AVRO HS-748: A LEGEND STILL AFLOAT AT 65. It will focus on the contribution of the aircraft to the IAF, its history, those who flew and maintained it and the 10 lakh flying hours it has completed.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: Indian Firm Ammunic Joins Indian Army’s Jet-Powered Drone Race
articles.text:
Bengaluru-based Ammunic Systems Private Limited has announced its interest in the Indian Army’s planned Jet Based Kamikaze Drone System by showing off an image of what appears to be their version of the system.
The Indian Army is moving towards conducting field trials of their indigenous Jet Based Kamikaze Drones at the Pokhran Field Firing Range in Rajasthan. The programme is planned to acquire a total of 540 drones valued at around ₹2,000 crore. The Army is looking to acquire the drones which can fly at speeds up to around 450 kmph.
Ammunic has shown an image of a streamlined, missile shaped drone with a pointed nose, swept wings and jet propulsion at the back. However, they have not given any specific details about the drone and have not confirmed if this is a flying prototype of the drone.
“We are closely monitoring the developments. Our experience in loitering munitions shows us the importance of electronics, integration and validation of systems to build a reliable weapon platform,” Ammunic said in an announcement.
The programme aims to give the Army greater access to high speed one way attack systems. Jet propulsion will allow the drone to fly much faster than traditional propeller driven loitering munitions. This will limit the amount of time an enemy air defence system will have to detect, track and engage the weapon.
The Indian Army’s Jet Based Kamikaze Drone System received Acceptance of Necessity from the Defence Acquisition Council in July 2026. As reported, the requirement is planned to be for 540 systems and valued at ₹2,000 crore. It has also been reported that 11 Indian companies have progressed through the qualification process.
However, there is no indication that Ammunic is one of these 11 companies, but they have stated that they are entering the race.
Ammunic Systems is a Defence R&D organisation specialising in advanced fuzing systems, warheads and weapon technologies. Moving into a jet powered drone will give them a more fully formed aerial weapon system to develop.
The company have not given any details about the range, payload, endurance, navigation, launch method or autonomy of the drone. They have also not announced any flight testing of the drone shown in the image.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: MiG-27 Procurement: Did Government Override IAF Concerns?
articles.text:
A former Indian Air Force crewman has rekindled the debate about why India chose to buy the Soviet-origin MiG-23BN and MiG-27 ML, stating that the Indian Air Force crewmen were not happy with the aircraft’s performance and the decision to acquire the MiG-23BN and MiG-27 ML was largely based on political decision making.
“When the Soviets proposed to upgrade our MiG-23BN to the MiG-27ML it was readily accepted by the Indian Air Force as it had better range, payload, avionics and handling,” the retired veteran stated in a post which has gone viral on social media.
However, he further claimed the crews were not happy with the aircraft’s performance. “Since the government had already decided to go ahead with the acquisition of the aircrafts, the reasons would be somewhere in the defence ministry files,”
the comments raise questions regarding how India’s military acquisitions were made during the Cold War, as the Soviet Union was one of India’s main defence partners.
The MiG-23BN was bought so that the Indian Air Force could have a specialised ground attack aircraft. This was later upgraded to the MiG-27ML, which was produced under licence by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited in Nashik.
The MiG-27 was built for ground attack missions. It had variable geometry wings, a powerful R-29 engine, and could carry a large amount of weapons externally. It had a large weapons payload.
The MiG-27ML had an upgraded navigation and attack system. The aircraft had the improved PrNK-23 navigation and attack complex.
The aircraft did have some issues such as being a single engine aircraft, and having high maintenance requirements. The aircraft also had aged analogue systems. However, the aircraft went through an extensive upgrade by HAL, DRDO and the Indian Air Force. It had upgraded avionics, navigation systems, cockpit and improved compatibility with precision guided weapons.
The upgraded MiG-27 was used during the 1999 Kargil conflict (Operation Safed Sagar), conducting ground attack sorties against the Pakistanis. It served in the Indian Air Force for many decades with the last squadron retiring the aircraft in December 2019.

Pakistan to Send Minister Musadik Malik to SCO Forum in New Delhi
articles.text:
Pakistan on Saturday announced that Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik would participate in the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum hosted by India at the historic Purana Qila in Delhi later this month.
The development comes a day after Union Culture Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat said that he was “hopeful” that Pakistan will also attend the event to be held here from November 20-22.
During an interaction with the press in New Delhi ahead of the event, the Union minister on Friday had announced that China, Kazakhstan, Iran, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan are among 15 countries that have confirmed participation in the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum.
India had announced on October 28 that invitations had been extended to all SCO members, including Pakistan, in keeping with established practice.
It was perhaps for the first time that New Delhi extended an invitation to a Pakistani minister to attend an event in India after last year’s May 7-10 military hostilities following Operation Sindoor.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi will attend the inaugural session of the SCO on November 20.
According to a statement by the Pakistan Foreign Office, the event would bring representatives from SCO member states to discuss issues related to civilisational dialogue and cultural understanding.
“The government of Pakistan remains committed to promoting dialogue among civilisations and fostering people-to-people contacts within the SCO framework in a spirit of mutual respect,” the statement said.
Musadik Malik is a key minister who frequently appears on talk shows to present the official version of the government.
His participation in the event hosted by India indicates that Pakistan wants to ease tensions with India to pave the way for its leadership to participate in the SCO summit being held in Islamabad next year.
Ties between the two countries have been strained following the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terror attack, which killed 26 people, and India’s subsequent launch of Operation Sindoor on May 7, targeting terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.
The military confrontation lasted four days and ended on May 10 following an understanding between the military officials of the two countries.
India has consistently raised the issue of cross-border terrorism at the SCO, maintaining that the grouping must adopt a united approach against terrorism and its financing, without double standards.
In Delhi, Shekhawat on Friday told reporters that Pakistan’s civilisational and cultural evolution is “not different from us”.
“It is less than 80 years only since they separated from us (referring to the 1947 Partition of the Indian subcontinent); their evolution has happened parallelly with us. Therefore, there doesn’t seem to be a possibility that they will have any differences over this (cultural civilisation) subject,” the Union minister said.
Shekhawat said there are geopolitical, strategic and bilateral relations, and “going a step further, (at this forum) there will be discussions on how we can reinforce a cultural relation, in coming time, and can establish a better dialogue and harmony between countries, and in between the people of the countries”.
The SCO was founded at a summit in Shanghai in 2001 by the presidents of Russia, China, the Kyrgyz Republic, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. India and Pakistan became its permanent members in 2017. Iran became a member in 2023.
Among the main goals of the SCO are to strengthen mutual trust, friendship and good-neighbourliness; and promote multilateral interaction to maintain and ensure peace, security and stability in the region, reads its website.
Besides its member countries, the SCO has some observer states and dialogue partners. There are 15 countries with SCO dialogue partner status, namely, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Bahrain, Egypt, Cambodia, Qatar, Kuwait, Laos, the Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Sri Lanka, according to the SCO website.
In October 2024, Islamabad hosted the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting, which Minister for External Affairs S Jaishankar attended on behalf of his prime minister.
India last month sent its SCO National Coordinator Alok Dimri to Islamabad for a preparatory meeting for the next SCO Council of Heads of State.

articles.title: Delhi AQI dips to 290, but relief may be brief
articles.text: Following days of toxic, post-Diwali smog blanketing the national capital, Delhi's air quality improved slightly to the 'poor' category on Sunday, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 290 by 4 pm.Across the city's 58 monitoring stations, 34 registered 'poor' air quality and 23 logged 'very poor', leaving only Delhi Cantonment in the 'moderate' zone. NSIT Dwarka recorded the capital's worst air, with an AQI of 364. Earlier that morning, the Sameer app had placed the city's air in the 'very poor' bracket at 350.Per the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) scale, an AQI of 0–50 is 'good', 51–100 is 'satisfactory', 101–200 is 'moderate', 201–300 is 'poor', 301–400 is 'very poor', and 401–500 is 'severe'. Delhi had been stuck in the 'very poor' tier continuously since November 11, with hourly readings repeatedly nearing, and once breaching, the 'severe' threshold. Prior to Sunday, the last 'poor' AQI reading was 299 on November 10, preceded by 261 on November 1.Real-time PM2.5 source apportionment data from the Air Quality Early Warning System and the Integrated Decision Support System identified biomass burning, encompassing stubble burning, domestic solid biofuels, wood, and dung cakes—as Sunday's primary pollutant source at 37.1 per cent. Secondary organic aerosols, which are fine particulates generated by atmospheric gas reactions, ranked second at 22 per cent, trailed by vehicular emissions (17.2 per cent) and secondary inorganic aerosols (9.6 per cent). Smaller shares came from waste burning, such as municipal, plastic, and rubber waste (5.5 per cent), mixed combustion (4.3 per cent), mineral dust and ash (2 per cent), firecrackers (1.6 per cent), and industrial emissions (0.6 per cent).This relief is expected to be brief. According to the Air Quality Early Warning System, Delhi's air will likely stay 'poor' on November 16 before deteriorating back to 'very poor' on November 17 and 18, remaining in that bracket for the following six days.Meteorologists credited Sunday's temporary dip in pollution to light rain and stronger winds helping disperse trapped pollutants. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) noted that parts of Delhi experienced drizzle or very light rain over the preceding 24 hours, accompanied by southwesterly surface winds peaking at 15 kmph. Skies were mostly cloudy before turning partly cloudy by afternoon, with southwesterly winds blowing up to 10 kmph.However, the IMD's forecast bulletin projects the city's ventilation index to drop steadily, from 16,000 square metres per second on November 15 to 15,000 on November 16, 7,500 on November 17, and 6,000 on November 18. The bulletin noted that a ventilation index below 6,000 square metres per second, combined with average wind speeds under 10 kmph, creates poor conditions for dispersing pollutants.

articles.title: Chinese Analysts Question India’s Two-Fighter Carrier Strategy
articles.text:
The maiden carrier landing for the Rafale-M fighter aircraft on the INS Vikrant on 29 October was a significant milestone for the Indian Navy. However, two reports from Chinese media highlight that the aircraft is a test version manufactured by Dassault and not the version ordered by India.
This was highlighted in Guancha’s exclusive report by 山猫. The article noted that the 26 Rafale-M aircraft ordered by India have not been delivered. The test aircraft pictured does not have any national markings, only the number ‘1’ on its wings. It can be seen that this aircraft is owned by the manufacturer, and flown by a Dassault pilot.
The images show the aircraft going through various stages of the trial, with at least one being a touch-and-go rather than arrested landing. After the successful landing, Indian Navy officers shook hands with the French pilot. This is an important point to note, as the event was a technical verification rather than the actual deployment of an Indian Navy squadron of Rafale-M aircraft. The report also discussed the lengthy procurement process for the Indian Navy. They released an RFI in 2017 for a new carrier-based fighter. This eventually came down to Boeing’s F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and Dassault’s Rafale-M.
Both aircraft were subjected to testing to see their compatibility with land-based ski jump operations at the Shore Based Test Facility in Goa, and the Rafale-M was chosen as the favourite. This became evident by the end of 2022.
On the 28th April 2025, an agreement was signed with France for 26 aircraft; 22 single-seat combat versions of the Rafale-M and 4 twin-seat trainers for land-based training. The deal is worth around ₹63,000 crore with weapons, equipment, training and logistics included. The deliveries are set to start at the end of 2028 and finish in 2030. There are also provisions set within the deal for the manufacturing of the Rafale airframe, and engine and sensor MRO facilities. These provisions are an attempt to build up an ecosystem around the fighter in India however this is not a full technology transfer. CNR questioned the integration.
Another report discussing the maiden carrier operation for the Rafale-M was aired by the CNR Military programme on China National Radio. The article was published on the 10th November in China Review News with the following headline;
“Rafale-M Makes Maiden Carrier Operation. What Does This Really Mean For Indian Aircraft Carrier?”
Military observer Shao Yongling stated that we shouldn’t confuse a successful test with actual capability for the Indian Navy. He outlined three key issues:
Training: The Rafale-M does not have a twin seat training aircraft for carrier operations. Indian Navy pilots currently fly the Russian MiG-29K, so will need to undergo conversion training to fly the French fighter. They will then need to become familiar with the ski jump launch system on INS Vikrant.
The aircraft was originally designed for the French Charles de Gaulle carrier which has catapult assisted take off and arrested landing capabilities. Vikrant has a STOBAR system. The aircraft will have weight and performance limitations due to the ski jump launch. Testing will need to be done to see how the aircraft performs with the carrier under different circumstances. Compatibility: Having two different aircraft will cause issues with having separate parts, maintenance, diagnostics and weapons handling systems on board. The MiG-29K does not have the same family of weapons as the Rafale-M, so the Rafale-M cannot just use Russian missiles. The Rafale-M does not have folding wings. The wings are around 10.9m wide compared to the 10m aircraft lifts on Vikrant.
The Navy are looking into modifications to allow them to fit the aircraft onto the carrier. This could affect how they move the aircraft between the hangar and deck. This can create issues with where the aircraft can be parked, and how they can be moved around the deck to produce sorties. Dual Track Strategy: The Rafale-M is supposed to be a stop gap solution for the Indian Navy whilst they develop their own twin engine deck based fighter. Shao stated that buying the French aircraft may take money away from developing their own aircraft domestically.
France will also not likely give them any of their most sensitive technologies. This means the Indian Navy may not get the best of both worlds. The CNR are not saying that the aircraft will not be able to operate from Vikrant, however they are questioning how quickly they can transition from a successful manufacturer test into a sustainable carrier air wing.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: India Must Move Beyond Technology Adoption, Says Rajnath Singh
articles.text:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Sunday called for making India not merely a user of advanced technologies, but also a developer, innovator, and global leader in critical domains, emphasising the need to strengthen the country’s Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) ecosystem to enhance defence preparedness and self-reliance.
Virtually addressing the 36th Annual Conference on Non-Destructive Evaluation & Enabling Technologies and the 15th International Symposium on Non-Destructive Testing in Aerospace, he stressed the importance of developing indigenous capabilities in advanced inspection technologies, promoting consistent quality assurance practices, and ensuring the accuracy, reliability and integrity of testing results, particularly in strategic applications.
The Defence Minister asserted that there can be no compromise on the integrity of testing results in strategic applications.
The three-day conference, organised by the Indian Society for Non-Destructive Testing in Hyderabad, has brought together over 2,000 professionals, researchers, industry experts and students to deliberate on the latest advancements, emerging technologies and applications in NDT.
Rajnath Singh stressed that NDT technologies enable examination of the integrity of materials, components and structures without causing any damage to them. Elucidating the concept, he said that just as ultrasound and X-rays help examine the human body without surgical intervention, NDT techniques enable the detection of internal defects in critical components without dismantling or damaging them.
He underlined that as Indian defence systems become increasingly sophisticated, every critical material, component, assembly and manufacturing process must meet the highest standards of quality and reliability. “Hidden defects can affect operational availability, increase maintenance requirements, reduce the service life of equipment and, in critical situations, jeopardise mission success. We need to move beyond a culture of merely identifying defects towards actively preventing them by embedding quality at every stage of the manufacturing process,” he said.
The Defence Minister stressed that the progress of a nation depends not merely on the technologies it develops, but also on the quality, reliability and security of the systems it builds. In defence applications, including missiles, aircraft, naval platforms and spacecraft, quality is not merely a manufacturing requirement but an essential element of operational reliability and national security, he said.
He noted that the field of Non-Destructive Evaluation is itself undergoing a major technological transformation. Technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Robotics, Advanced Sensors, Digital Twins, and Predictive Analytics are significantly expanding the possibilities of inspection and structural health monitoring. These technologies can improve the speed and consistency of inspections, assist in analysing complex data and identify patterns that may not be easily detectable through conventional methods, he said.
Rajnath Singh observed that the future lies in the intelligent integration of these proven inspection techniques with advanced digital technologies. Such integration can make inspection processes more accurate, efficient and responsive to emerging industrial requirements.
“India must not limit itself to merely adopting these technologies. We must also develop indigenous solutions tailored to our strategic and industrial requirements. By investing in research, advanced equipment, software and skilled manpower, we can strengthen our domestic capabilities and develop technologies that can find demand in international markets as well,” he said.
“We must strengthen our indigenous capabilities in advanced inspection technologies, specialised sensors, evaluation equipment and associated software. Developing domestic capabilities in these areas is essential for reducing technological dependencies and securing critical defence supply chains. We must promote consistent quality assurance practices across the entire defence industrial ecosystem. Public Sector Undertakings, private manufacturers, start-ups and MSMEs have an important role to play in this endeavour. We must ensure that inspection results are accurate, reliable and traceable, and are based on robust procedures and appropriate standards followed by assessment by qualified professionals,” he added.
Highlighting India’s growing indigenous defence ecosystem, Rajnath Singh cited achievements in missile development, naval platforms, aerospace engineering, radar systems and space applications as reflections of the expanding scientific and industrial capabilities of the nation. He described the commissioning of India’s first indigenous aircraft carrier, INS Vikrant, as an important milestone in the Aatmanirbhar Bharat journey.
Source: IANS

A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Crypto’s slow-motion selloff leaves traders weary and hopeless
articles.text: Bitcoin’s latest selloff is testing the resolve of some of the cryptocurrency market’s most committed investors, as a succession of setbacks pushes prices toward their lowest levels of the year and major sources of demand weaken.The largest digital asset fell toward $62,000 in weekend trading, reaching its weakest level since July, extending a decline that has gathered pace in recent weeks. Unlike the abrupt crashes that have punctuated previous crypto downturns, much of the preceding decline unfolded during relatively subdued trading before liquidations accelerated in recent days.The steady erosion is adding to a sense of exhaustion across a market confronting a growing list of obstacles, from the record hack at Binance and renewed political uncertainty following Democratic gains in the US midterm elections to rising Treasury yields and a stronger dollar. Meanwhile, the artificial-intelligence boom and Anthropic’s upcoming IPO are competing for money and attention once directed toward digital assets.“The near-term direction will largely depend on whether institutional demand stabilizes and macro conditions provide room for risk appetite to recover,” said Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer at Monarq Asset Management. “Until then, rallies are likely to remain fragile and volatility elevated.”135852805US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which helped draw Wall Street investors into the market, have become another source of selling pressure. From Oct. 30 — the day after the Binance hack — through Nov. 13, the ETFs saw almost $3 billion in net outflows.Economic conditions offer little relief. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries has climbed above 5% as persistent inflation fueled expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy. Higher yields raise the opportunity cost of holding assets that generate no income, while the stronger dollar has added pressure to Bitcoin and gold.Crypto-specific developments have compounded the weakness.The Binance hack has revived questions about the security of trading platforms at a time when the industry is struggling to rebuild investor confidence. The competition for speculative capital is also intensifying. Anthropic’s planned initial public offering has attracted heavy demand ahead of its expected listing, raising the possibility that investors are freeing up money from other holdings, including cryptocurrencies, to participate. The extent of any direct shift out of digital assets remains unclear.“Theories around the market weakness tend to focus on the large outflows of stablecoin balances, nearly $20 billion over the last month, the upcoming IPO of Anthropic and its impact on liquidity,” said Joshua Lim, co-head of markets at FalconX.Bitcoin’s retreat is particularly frustrating for investors who had expected mainstream adoption to provide a more durable foundation for prices. Major financial institutions have expanded their involvement in digital assets, and ETFs have made Bitcoin available to a much broader pool of investors. Those advances have not insulated the market from its latest downturn.Many smaller digital tokens have surrendered years of gains, challenging the returns available to investors who held through successive industry booms and busts.For traders looking for a potential floor, August offers one reference point.After risk appetite improved following the US Treasury’s announcement of an increase in long-bond buybacks, Bitcoin rallied from below $65,000 to above $87,000 by late September. The latest decline has erased most of those gains and raised the prospect of a further slide under the roughly $58,000 level that has marked this year’s low.“We’re in a risk-off environment across all financial markets. Interest rates keep rising with the war still pressuring inflation,” said Ryan Watkins, co-founder of crypto investment fund Syncracy Capital.

LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in
articles.text:
Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all.

The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children.

The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories."

Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids.

Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it.

LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013. It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge.

The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011. The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory.

The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948.

EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I. ®
